name: Claw Ride
keyCorrections: If they keep sitting up: your chest pressure is not enough — drive your chest deeper into their upper back
If they turn into you: switch to the back take immediately — do not stay in the claw
If you lose the claw grip: re-establish it by reaching deeper around their hip
description: Use arm and chest clamps around the hip line or torso from turtle, build base, and secure back exposure through hip switches and hand fighting. The claw ride is a transitional control system that uses leg and arm clamps to break down the turtle position.
shortInstruction: From turtle, clamp your near arm around their hip (claw grip), drive your chest into their ribs, and walk your hips to the side to collapse their base. Switch between claw and back take as they react.
summary: The claw ride uses a deep arm clamp around the opponent's hip or lower torso to break down the turtle position and expose the back. The claw grip (arm wrapped around the hip, hand gripping the far hip or belt line) creates a structural lever that allows you to pull the opponent flat while your chest pressure prevents them from posturing up. The system alternates between claw pressure and back take attempts, forcing the opponent to defend one and expose the other.
whyItWorks: The claw grip on the far hip creates a lever that pulls the opponent's base out from under them — they cannot posture up when their hip is pulled toward you
Chest pressure on their ribs prevents them from sitting up or turning into you — the two primary turtle escapes
Alternating between claw pressure and back take attempts creates a dilemma — if they defend the claw, they expose the back
The claw ride works from both sides — you can switch your claw to the opposite hip without losing pressure
commonMistakes: Clamping too high on the torso instead of the hip — a torso clamp can be escaped by sitting through
Letting your chest separate from their back — chest connection is what prevents them from posturing up
Staying in the claw ride too long without transitioning — the claw ride is a transitional control, not a pin
Not protecting your own head — the opponent can sit through and take your back if your head is on the far side without control
coachingCues: Claw on the hip, not the ribs
safetySummary: Do not apply sudden rotational pressure to the opponent's spine when collapsing the turtle — use slow, controlled pressure
If the opponent rolls out of the claw ride suddenly, protect your head and neck
Be aware of your fingers when clawing — fingers caught between the mat and the opponent's body can be injured

systemLogic.corePrinciple: The claw ride is a three-phase system: Establish Claw: Collapse Turtle → Back Take

decisionTree.action: from behind the turtle, reach your near arm around their hip and grip their far hip crease or belt. Your chest should be connected to their upper back or shoulder blade
drive your chest down into their back while pulling their hip toward you with the claw grip. Walk your knees toward their head to flatten them. They should roll onto their hip or side
as they collapse, release the claw grip and replace it with a seatbelt (arm over the far shoulder, hand on the near hip). Slide your near knee into their hip line and secure back control

decisionTree.condition: they resist the collapse by posturing hard
decisionTree.action: switch your grip to the near wrist and use the spiral ride to collapse them instead. The claw ride and spiral ride are complementary systems

moneyDetails: The claw ride is the primary turtle-breaking system in modern wrestling and BJJ — every grappler who trains to break the turtle uses this system
Mastering the claw ride gives you a reliable path from turtle to back control — the most dominant position in grappling
The claw ride works against larger opponents because it uses leverage (pulling the hip) rather than strength
fixItFast: If they sit up despite your claw: switch to a collar tie and drive their head to the mat — head control beats posture every time
If they roll toward you: release the claw and take the back
If they roll away from you: follow them, maintain the claw, and drive your chest into their back
